artifactEvidence.excerpt: SB 1168 tells the California Public Utilities Commission to assess opportunities for rate structures — the rules used to divide charges among customer groups. The assessment must consider data centres’ reasonable share of transmission and distribution costs, their proportionate share of load and procurement costs, and pressure on residential customers.

The Energy Commission must publish submitted information annually in anonymized and aggregated form: combined so the public release does not expose one customer’s protected data. Its first specified statewide data-centre load-trend assessment belongs in the 2029 integrated energy policy report.

“Assess opportunities” is the important phrase. The law starts work inside a new or existing commission proceeding. It does not select a tariff, calculate a household saving or show how a particular utility will divide costs.

explainBack.question: A neighbour says: 'California just signed a law to protect ratepayers from data centres, so why is my October bill identical?' What is the causal answer?
explainBack.answer: Because SB 1168 only orders the Public Utilities Commission to assess opportunities for rate structures inside a new or existing proceeding. An assessment is a study step, not a tariff. Bills change only after the commission finishes a proceeding and approves an actual rate dividing costs among customer groups, and no such rate has been adopted. AB 1577 changes visibility, not prices: covered facilities file estimates at permitting and report to the state after energization, published only in anonymized aggregate.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: The answer should cite the operative verb 'assess opportunities', the proceeding-then-rate sequence, and the distinction between reporting duties and price changes, as in P003, P004 and P007.
explainBack.assessment: The article's mechanism fully supports this answer in ordinary language; the operative-verb framing in P004 does the decisive work. Pass.

unseenTransfer.scenario: In 2027, a developer proposes a 60 MW data centre outside Bakersfield needing a county conditional-use permit. A city councilmember asks a resident researcher what public information will exist about the facility's electricity use, and when state publications will reflect it.
unseenTransfer.question: Using only this article's mechanism, what can the resident expect to find, where, and what will not be publicly available?
unseenTransfer.answer: Because the facility exceeds 10 MW and is private, AB 1577 covers it. At the discretionary permit stage the owner must submit usage estimates to the county, so local permit records will hold planning facts. After energization the owner reports specified information to the Energy Commission, then at least annually. The public will see that data only in anonymized, aggregated annual publications — no facility-level dossier — and statewide load-trend analysis first appears in the 2029 integrated energy policy report. Any bill effect would still require a separate CPUC proceeding and approved rate.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: Correct application of the 10 MW threshold and exclusions (P005, P007), permit-stage vs post-energization reporting (P005), and aggregate-only publication with 2029 timing (P006).
unseenTransfer.assessment: The article supplies every element needed to solve this novel scenario, including the negative result (no facility-level public data). The mechanism transfers cleanly. Pass.
